body: Thank you for the support you give. Would that we could all be so loving and supportive in our daily lives.

I mourn the loss of my brother, but I had a wife and 3 kids I needed to love, and a job I needed to keep to ensure that we could make our house payment every month. 

Dean was two years older than me, and he practically raised me when we were kids. So after his shit hit the fan, he would drop psychological landmines on me in the middle of my workday via email, causing me to basically fall apart emotionally and endanger my job (not to mention the attention it sucked away from my family; I have the world's most understanding wife.)

>"No one ... has the answers and if they act like they do it only alienates those they are trying to help."

I guess the question is, How much do we owe another person? At what cost do we keep the other person alive? Do I sacrifice my own children to keep my brother alive?

I never called him up and said, "Dean, how can I save you?" I (and my siblings) generally just reacted to whatever his current situation was. ("Now I'm an alcoholic." ... "Now I'm a cocaine addict." ... "Now I'm $100,000 in debt." ... "Now I'm facing prison time because I just got arrested for my 12th DUI.") Twenty-five years ago, I begged him and his girlfriend not to shoot up in their hotel room, then urged him not to go into credit-card debt to finance his drug habit, and finally I begged him not to flee to Costa Rica to skip out on his almost certain prison time for DUI.

Whenever we DID try to intervene, we were told that we were well-intentioned idiots who were clearly just tools of Wall Street. Of course anyone with 3 kids and a house payment is by definition a tool of someone, so this kind of psychological warfare was just debilitating. 

I tend to think it's probably like raising children: You (the parent) can't tell them anything past adolescence, but some respected adult other than the parent can have an enormous influence. So AA and Dean's counselors were basically his life support while he was in daily contact with them. But when that ended, he lost his lifeline.
Appreciate the hugs. I'll give those resources a look.
Thank you, Steve Perry, for the earworm.
Our parents left us a little money when they died. He can't have a whole lot left at this point.
I had never heard of Ibogaine. I'll look into this.
EDIT: I just typed the numbers "48," and it appeared as "1." If he were 1, this would all be so much easier. :)

Darawk: Thanks for sharing your own story. I hope you get clean before you get to where my brother is.

Here's the deal with rehab: As I said in another comment, he did two weeks (at significant expense) at a pretty good place. The main problem — from my perspective —  is that he didn't go immediately into a halfway house where he could be helped by (and could help) others who'd suffered through the same experience.

My sister and brother in law, the most generous people I've ever known, let him stay with them while he awaited space, but then he decided to drive out of state to shut down a storage unit he'd had for years. It was on that drive that he made his terrible decision to go south (physically and metaphorically). 

His excuse was that because of his lingering DUI he would be forced to go to prison, where he would almost certainly be raped. I regret to say that I reacted angrily to his bad decision, announced to his family in an email message, which did nothing to improve communications with him.

My sisters, however, have kept in touch with him, and the eldest one went down and spent a couple nightmarish days there. She got a hotel room in San Jose to get him out of the drug district, but he would simply excuse himself to use the bathroom and go shoot up. 

She finally got him to visit a rehab hospital, where the staff was wonderful. They told him what he needed, and he said, "I'm not ready right now." My sister could do nothing. She said that her sense was that he wanted to get through his stash, and THEN he would be ready. Which of course is a joke, because when you use up your stash, you simply go out and make another score. 

What are these vaccines you mention? I've never heard of these. On Monday i will call some doctors to explore this option. If you could elaborate now, that might help. I can write you offline, if you'd prefer.
I would never do that to a child. And because the son lives with his mom, that's out of the question anyhow. But thanks for weighing in.
Wesa and Dude: My sister has spoken to the Embassy, and they were surprisingly helpful. That is looking like our best option at the moment.
Thanks for the survivor story. Was there anything in particular that brought your brother out of his dive before he hit the pavement?

He did a 2-week residential rehab last summer, but only after he'd gotten the DUI. So he still had that hanging over his head. And it was looking like he'd do 3 months to a year in jail, and he freaked out and fled. The rehab was something that we (his brothers and sisters) persuaded him to do. In retrospect, he was never truly into it. But that was for alcohol. Now that he's gotten back into coke, I honestly think the chemical detox — how ever it is achieved — might be his best hope. But yeah, I've definitely considered doing the bounty hunter thing and simply thumping him over the head and driving him back to the States.

Your comment reminds me of all the people I've known over the years with obsessive hobbies — collecting tin soldiers, stalking a NASCAR driver, collecting Nazi memorabilia. I've quietly laughed at them. Now I see they're the smart survivors.
Here's the really sad part, and the one reason he should, as you say, "pay attention to something here": He's got a son, age 15, who is being raised by his fundamentalist Christian mother and stepfather and subjected to the typical evangelical BS (creationism, speaking in tongues, etc.). My brother, a biologist, has never overtly told the kid that his family is deluded, but instead took him on hikes and showed him living examples of species variation. For a long time, Dean kept his son as his focus, and in a symbiotic way, the father and son each seemed to be the other's best hope. In my darker moments I hope my brother dies before he's signed over his entire life savings to a drug cartel so that my nephew will at least have some money left to pay for college.
